newsitem.title: USA: FBI reopens 1963 black church bombing investigation.
newsitem.headline: FBI reopens 1963 black church bombing investigation.

text.p: The FBI has reopened its investigation into the infamous 1963 Klan bombing of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, which killed four young black girls, federal officials said on Thursday.

Investigators reopened the case a year ago and say they have received credible new information about the Sunday attack, which symbolised the violent cruelty of Southern white resistance to the civil rights movement of the 1960s.

"The investigation has been conducted in a covert fashion," FBI spokesman Craig Dahle said. "The reason it's now become public is that we started interviewing witnesses yesterday, and we knew word would get out sooner or later."

Dahle declined to comment when asked if investigators had any new suspects, saying only that the FBI had conducted a review of existing evidence and received new "information over a relatively recent period of time."
The bomb, which exploded at the predominantly black church Sept. 15, 1963, cut short the lives of Denise McNair, 11, and Cynthia Wesley, Carole Robertson and Addie Mae Collins, all 14.
Ku Klux Klansman Robert Edward Chambliss was convicted of the bombing in 1977 and died in jail eight years later, aged 81. But authorities suspected at least three other men were involved.

In Washington, Attorney General Janet Reno confirmed an investigation was being pursued as vigorously as possible, based on new information, but declined to predict whether indictments would be brought.

"When something that horrible occurs, I just want to make sure that we do everything humanly possible, and do it the right way, to see that people who do that sort of thing are held accountable," she said at her weekly news briefing.

Last month black American film director Spike Lee released a new documentary about the bombing. Entitled "Four Little Girls," the film retold the story of the case through the eyes of survivors and witnesses.
The FBI said its renewed investigation had nothing to do with the documentary.
